chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Working Capital Really Is

lessons.title: Why Working Capital Decides Whether a Business Survives

children.text: Meet Rakesh. He runs a precision auto-components unit in Nashik that supplies brackets and machined parts to a large two-wheeler maker. Last year his profit and loss statement showed a healthy ₹1.2 crore profit. His order book is the fullest it has ever been. And on the 28th of this month, he is on the phone with his bank manager, asking for an extension on his limit because he cannot pay 140 workers their salaries on the 1st.

Nothing is wrong with Rakesh's product, his margins or his customer. What is wrong is timing. His money is sitting in steel on his shop floor and in invoices his customer has not yet paid. This lesson is about that trapped money, and why managing it decides whether a business survives.

body.text: Profit tells you whether a business makes money. Working capital tells you whether it has the money when the bills arrive. Businesses rarely die from a lack of profit. They die from running out of cash while waiting for profit to turn into cash.

children.text: What Working Capital Actually Is
Every business that sells a physical product or delivers a service on credit has to put money into its operations before it gets money back. That money is its
working capital
. On a balance sheet, it shows up as the difference between two groups of items.

markDefs.definition: The money a business needs to run its day-to-day operations: current assets such as inventory, receivables and cash, minus current liabilities such as amounts owed to suppliers.

children.text: The first group is
current assets
: cash in the bank, raw material and finished goods lying in the warehouse, and
receivables
, the money customers owe you. The second group is
current liabilities
payables
owed to suppliers, short-term bank borrowings, salaries and taxes due within the year.

markDefs.definition: Assets the business expects to turn into cash or use up within 12 months, such as cash, inventory and money owed by customers.
Money customers owe the business for goods or services already delivered on credit. Also called debtors or trade receivables.
Obligations the business must pay within 12 months, such as supplier bills, short-term loans, salaries due and taxes payable.
Money the business owes its suppliers for goods or services already received on credit. Also called creditors or trade payables.

body.caption: Net working capital: what the business has tied up in day-to-day operations after counting what it owes in the short term

children.text: If Rakesh has ₹4 crore in current assets and ₹2.5 crore in current liabilities, his working capital is ₹1.5 crore. That ₹1.5 crore has to come from somewhere: his own capital, retained profits or a bank limit. It is money that cannot be used to buy a new CNC machine, repay a term loan or pay a dividend, because it is busy keeping the factory running.

body.text: You will meet more precise versions of this formula later in the course, such as gross working capital and operating working capital. For now, hold on to the simple idea: working capital is the money locked inside the business's daily cycle.

children.text: The Cycle That Traps the Cash
The easiest way to see working capital is to follow one rupee through Rakesh's business. He buys steel on 30-day credit, turns it into brackets, ships them, and waits for his customer to pay.

events.title: Steel arrives
events.description: Rakesh receives ₹10 lakh of steel from a Pune distributor on 30-day credit. No cash has left yet.

events.title: Supplier is paid
events.description: The distributor's credit period ends. ₹10 lakh leaves Rakesh's bank account. The brackets are still being machined and finished.

events.title: Brackets are dispatched
events.description: Finished goods finally leave the factory with an invoice. Between Day 0 and Day 45 the order sat as inventory.

events.title: Customer pays
events.description: The two-wheeler maker pays on its standard 75-day terms. Cash finally comes back in.

children.text: Rakesh paid out cash on Day 30 and got it back on Day 120. For 90 days, his own money funded his customer's supply chain. This gap is called the
cash conversion cycle
, and you will calculate it properly in Chapter 2.

markDefs.definition: The number of days between paying cash out for inputs and collecting cash back from customers: inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days.

body.title: How long is the cash stuck?
body.prompt: A garment exporter in Tiruppur holds fabric and finished stock for 60 days, gives its overseas buyer 45 days to pay, and gets 40 days of credit from its yarn supplier. For how many days is the exporter's cash tied up in each order?
body.explanation: Cash is tied up for inventory days plus customer credit days, minus supplier credit days: 60 + 45 - 40 = 65 days. The longer this number, the more working capital every rupee of sales needs.

children.text: Why Growth Can Break a Profitable Business

Here is the part that surprises most founders. Growth consumes cash before it produces it. Every extra rupee of sales needs extra inventory and extra receivables, and those have to be funded upfront. Profit arrives later, and only partly as cash.
Take a simple business where working capital is 25% of sales and cash profit is 8% of sales. Watch what happens when sales double two years in a row and then stop growing. All figures are in ₹ crore.

body.caption: Profit vs the extra working capital growth demands (₹ crore)

body.title: Cash profit vs extra working capital needed (₹ crore)

children.text: In Years 2 and 3 the business is more profitable than ever, yet it is short of ₹0.9 crore and then ₹1.8 crore of cash. Only in Year 4, when growth pauses, does profit finally show up in the bank. A founder who does not see this coming will think the business is failing at the exact moment it is succeeding.

body.text: Growing faster than you can fund your working capital has a name: overtrading. It is one of the most common reasons fast-growing Indian SMEs default on their bank limits, even while their sales and profits look excellent.

body.title: Spot the cash crunch
body.question: Which of these is most likely to push a profitable, well-run business into a cash crunch?
options: A one-time rise in its depreciation charge
Doubling sales to new customers who demand 90-day credit
Paying its suppliers on the due date instead of early
Keeping inventory at the same level as last year
body.explanation: Rapid growth on long credit terms means the business must fund a much bigger pile of receivables and inventory before any of that new revenue arrives as cash. Depreciation is a non-cash charge, and paying suppliers on time or holding inventory flat do not add new strain.

children.text: Two Indian Extremes: HUL and Titan

Working capital needs vary enormously across businesses. Look at how many days of cash each of these listed companies has locked in its cycle, as reported in the Ratios section of screener.in for FY2026.

stats.label: Hindustan Unilever
stats.context: Cash conversion cycle, FY2026. Suppliers effectively fund HUL.

stats.label: Avenue Supermarts (DMart)
stats.context: Cash conversion cycle, FY2026. Near-instant customer collections.

stats.label: Titan Company
stats.context: Cash conversion cycle, FY2026. Gold jewellery inventory is huge.

body.title: Why the two ends look so different

columns.label: Hindustan Unilever
points: Sells soaps, detergents and tea that move off shelves in days
Distributors pay quickly, so debtor days are only about 19
Its scale lets it take long credit from suppliers: about 169 payable days
Result: it collects from customers before it pays suppliers

columns.label: Titan Company
points: Jewellery stores must display a wide range of designs in gold
Inventory days run to about 222, as gold sits in stores and workshops
Customers pay at the counter, so debtor days are tiny
Result: the business must fund months of inventory before selling it

body.title: Wait, is Titan in trouble with a 211-day cycle?

children.text: No. A long cycle is not automatically bad. It means the business needs a lot of funding for its operations, and the question is how it arranges that funding. Screener.in also shows Titan's working capital days at only about 28 for FY2026, far lower than its cash conversion cycle.

The difference comes from current liabilities that are not trade payables. Jewellers like Titan commonly finance part of their gold through gold metal loans from banks, and collect advances from customers through jewellery purchase schemes. Both sit in current liabilities and fund the inventory. A healthy business with a long cycle has planned how to fund it. A struggling one discovers the gap when a bill bounces.
When the Cycle Breaks: India's Delayed Payment Problem

Working capital stress rarely stays inside one company. When a large buyer pays late, its delay becomes its supplier's working capital problem, and that supplier then pays its own vendors late. This chain is especially painful for small businesses, which have the least bargaining power and the most expensive borrowing.

body.label: Delayed payments owed to Indian MSMEs
body.context: Down from ₹10.7 lakh crore in 2022, according to the Delayed Payments Report 3.0 by GAME, FISME and C2FO. Still a massive amount of small-business cash stuck in someone else's cycle.

children.text: The power sector shows the same pattern at a larger scale. State electricity distribution companies owed generators about ₹1.39 lakh crore in June 2022, when the Centre notified the Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules, 2022. Those rules let defaulting distribution companies be restricted from buying power on exchanges, and outstanding dues fell sharply within a year. For power producers, that was a direct release of trapped working capital.

body.text: This is also why the government created TReDS platforms and the MSME 45-day payment rule. Both are covered in detail later in this course.

children.text: Why This Is Not Just the Finance Team's Problem

Working capital is created by decisions made across the company, most of them outside the finance department. If you work in sales, procurement, operations or HR, you are already managing working capital, whether you know it or not.

body.caption: Everyday decisions that move working capital

cells: Offering 90-day credit instead of 30 to close a deal
Receivables rise, more cash locked up
Bulk-buying six months of raw material for a discount
Inventory rises, more cash locked up
Payables rise, less cash locked up
Cutting production lead time from 20 days to 12
Paying annual bonuses in one lump sum in April
A large short-term liability that must be funded on one date

body.title: The big order that could sink you
body.scenario: You head sales at a Coimbatore pump manufacturer that currently gives customers 30 days of credit. A large infrastructure contractor offers a ₹5 crore annual order at a 12% profit margin, but insists on 90-day payment terms. Your company funds its working capital through a bank cash credit limit at 11% interest a year, and the limit is already 85% used.
body.prompt: Should you accept the order on these terms? Work out the extra working capital required and its cost, and suggest what you would negotiate.
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the extra receivables. At 30 days, a ₹5 crore annual order keeps about ₹41.1 lakh outstanding at any time (₹5 crore x 30 / 365). At 90 days, that rises to about ₹123.3 lakh. So the order needs roughly ₹82.2 lakh of extra working capital, before counting any extra inventory.

Funded through the cash credit limit at 11%, that costs about ₹9.04 lakh a year. The order still earns ₹60 lakh of profit, so it remains profitable on paper.

The real problem is cash, not profit. With the limit already 85% used, finding ₹82 lakh of headroom may be impossible, and one delayed payment from the contractor could push the company over its limit.

What to negotiate: ask for 60-day terms, or a price increase of about 1.8% to cover the financing cost, or check whether the contractor will accept invoices on a TReDS platform so you can get paid early. Only accept 90 days if the bank agrees to enhance the limit first. Profitable orders that the business cannot fund are how good companies end up like Rakesh.

body.text: A useful habit for anyone outside finance: before agreeing to longer credit or bigger stock, ask "how much cash does this lock up, and for how long?" That single question changes the quality of commercial decisions.

children.text: Lock In the Vocabulary

cards.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities. The money tied up in running the business day to day.
Cash, inventory, receivables and other assets expected to turn into cash or be used up within 12 months.
Supplier payables, short-term borrowings, salaries and taxes due within 12 months.
Money customers owe for goods or services already delivered on credit.
Money the business owes suppliers for goods or services already received on credit.
Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. How long cash stays locked in operations.
Growing sales faster than the business can fund the extra working capital, causing a cash crunch despite profits.

body.title: Complete the formula
body.textWithBlank: Working capital equals current assets minus current ___.
body.explanation: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. The larger the gap, the more money is tied up in the business's daily operations.

body.description: Scroll to the Ratios section to see debtor days, inventory days, days payable and the cash conversion cycle for the last 12 years. Then search for a company in your own industry and compare.

points: Working capital is the money locked in day-to-day operations: current assets minus current liabilities.
A business pays for inputs before it collects from customers, and that timing gap is what creates the need for working capital.
Rapid growth consumes cash, because extra inventory and receivables must be funded before profit arrives. This is how profitable companies run out of money.
Working capital needs vary hugely: HUL runs a negative cash conversion cycle while Titan's runs past 200 days, and both can be healthy if funded well.
Late payments pass stress down the supply chain, which is why delayed dues to MSMEs remain a multi-lakh-crore problem in India.
Sales, procurement, operations and HR decisions all create or release working capital, so everyone in the business shares responsibility for it.
